Subject: Trail etiquette: the unwritten rules, written down
Preview: A practical guide to sharing the trail without making it weird.
Body: You already know the outdoors. This is just a reminder of what makes shared trails work.

YIELD ORDER

Hikers yield to horses. Bikes yield to hikers. Everyone yields to horses. On a narrow switchback, the person going uphill has the right of way — they're working harder and have less visibility ahead.

PASS WITH A HEADS-UP

Say something before you close the gap. "On your left" or a simple "passing" is enough. Silence followed by sudden presence startles people and animals alike. Give at least 6 feet when passing equestrians and step to the downhill side so you appear smaller.

CAMP AND STEP SETBACKS

Camp at least 200 feet from lakes, streams, and trails. That's roughly 70 adult paces. The same 200-foot rule applies when you need to answer a call of nature. Catholes should be 6 to 8 inches deep.

NOISE ON THE TRAIL

Keep group conversations trail-width — sound carries farther than you think in open terrain. Earbuds in both ears mean you won't hear a mountain biker or a ranger calling out. One earbud, or none.

DOG PROTOCOL

Leash rules exist for wildlife corridors, not just nervous dogs. A 6-foot leash gives you actual control. Pick up after your dog even when no one is watching — especially then.

LEAVE THE TRAIL BETTER

If you pack it in, pack it out. That includes orange peels, apple cores, and nut shells — they take months to break down at elevation and attract animals to the trail corridor.

WIDEN YOUR FOOTPRINT AWARENESS

On established trails, walk single-file and stay on the surface even when it's muddy. Going around mud widens the trail. Wear the mud.

That's the short version. Most of it comes down to slowing down enough to notice who else is out there.
